title: How schoolteachers helped shape early experimental psychology in Britain.
author: Marc Smith
summary: Marc Smith complicates the tidy story that experimental psychology travelled from German laboratories to Britain through a handful of famous academics. He shows that the early British discipline was fragmented and that schoolteachers and other amateurs helped build it. Joseph Jacobs replicated Ebbinghaus's memory method in 1887 with pupils at North London Collegiate School, assisted by the headmistress Sophie Bryant and advised by James Sully, who wrote the Teacher's Handbook of Psychology and drew on his contact with teachers. Teachers and parents also formed the British Child Study Association in 1893, and William Henry Winch ran school-based research through a network of amateur researchers, work that helped lead to the appointment of Cyril Burt in 1913. Smith links this to the 2010s, when teachers connected through social media again took up Ebbinghaus, transfer and retrieval practice, and he wonders how far this movement has in turn shaped modern psychology.
points: The early British discipline was piecemeal and local, so the usual transmission story from Leipzig and Berlin to Cambridge hides the people who actually carried the ideas into schools.
Jacobs's 1887 replication of Ebbinghaus took only two years to appear and was run in a girls' school with a teacher, Sophie Bryant, as collaborator.
James Sully revised his Teacher's Handbook of Psychology largely because of his contact with teachers and training institutions, so demand from classrooms helped shape the content.
Winch's network of teacher researchers produced school-based data that later mattered to academic psychologists and fed into the creation of the first official educational psychologist post.
Today's teacher interest in retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving repeats the pattern, and may be steering research topics as well as book sales.
quotes: But the established academics weren’t the only individuals attempting to build the fledgling discipline. There were also the ‘mere amateurs’ (Gustavsson, 2026), many of whom were schoolteachers.

In his introduction to the fourth edition, Sully explains that the changes came about primarily through his contact with teachers and teacher training institutions. Educationalists were becoming increasingly interested in the application of psychology to teaching and learning, including aspects of cognition.

Jacobs, at the time, wasn’t an academic or associated with any university. Sophie Bryant was a teacher at North London Collegiate School (she would become headmistress there in 1895), and had been awarded the degree of Doctor of Science in 1884, the first woman in the UK to receive it.

Despite these historical creases, as early as at least 1887, teachers were involved in the establishment and growth of experimental psychology and potentially the transfer of this knowledge into education and training.

Winch carried out his research in schools with the help of schoolteachers, creating his own network of amateur researchers and collecting data that would eventually become relevant to academic experimental psychologists.

Teachers certainly did shape early experimental psychology to some extent, but we may not fully appreciate how much their contemporaries have shifted the trajectory of modern psychology for some time.
